full_text:
दिल्ली-एनसीआर में इस समय भीषण गर्मी और उमस ने लोगों का जीना दूभर कर रखा है। लगातार 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक तापमान और गर्म हवाओं के कारण दिन के समय बाहर निकलना चुनौतीपूर्ण बना हुआ है। हालांकि, मौसम विभाग (आईएमडी) के ताजा पूर्वानुमान ने लोगों को राहत की उम्मीद दी है।
विभाग के अनुसार, अगले कुछ दिनों में मौसम का मिजाज बदलने वाला है और मानसून की गतिविधियां तेज होने के साथ दिल्ली-एनसीआर में बारिश का सिलसिला शुरू हो सकता है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 29 और 30 जून को दिल्ली-एनसीआर में अधिकतम तापमान 41 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहने की संभावना है। इन दो दिनों के दौरान तेज धूप और उमस लोगों को परेशान करेगी। हालांकि, आसमान में आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहने के साथ शाम या रात के समय कुछ इलाकों में हल्की बूंदाबांदी, धूल भरी आंधी और तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं। इससे तापमान में मामूली गिरावट महसूस हो सकती है, लेकिन व्यापक राहत मिलने की संभावना कम है।
मौसम वैज्ञानिकों का कहना है कि 1 जुलाई यानी बुधवार से मौसम में बड़ा बदलाव देखने को मिल सकता है। इस दिन से दिल्ली और आसपास के क्षेत्रों में गरज-चमक के साथ हल्की से मध्यम बारिश शुरू होने का अनुमान है। कई स्थानों पर तेज हवाओं के साथ बारिश होने की भी संभावना जताई गई है। बारिश का यह दौर गर्मी और उमस से राहत दिलाएगा तथा अधिकतम तापमान में 3 से 5 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक की गिरावट दर्ज की जा सकती है। इसके बाद दिन का तापमान 35 से 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहने की संभावना है, जिससे मौसम पहले की तुलना में काफी सुहावना हो जाएगा। मानसून को लेकर भी अच्छी खबर सामने आई है।
मौसम विशेषज्ञों के अनुसार, अगले 5 से 6 दिनों के भीतर दक्षिण-पश्चिम मानसून के दिल्ली-एनसीआर में पूरी तरह सक्रिय होने की संभावना है। यदि मौजूदा परिस्थितियां अनुकूल बनी रहती हैं तो मानसून जल्द ही पूरे क्षेत्र को कवर कर लेगा। इसके बाद रुक-रुक कर बारिश का दौर जारी रह सकता है, जिससे भीषण गर्मी से लोगों को राहत मिलेगी और वातावरण में ठंडक बढ़ेगी। (इनपुट-आईएएनएस)

मौसम विभाग ने इस दिन आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहने का पूर्वानुमान जारी किया है। इसके बाद 26 जून को फिर से गरज के साथ बारिश की संभावना जताई गई है। इस दिन अधिकतम तापमान 40 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 28 डिग्री सेल्सियस रह सकता है। वहीं, 27 जून को भी गरज-चमक और बारिश की गतिविधियां देखने को मिल सकती हैं। इस दिन तापमान 40 और 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहने का अनुमान है। 28 जून को आसमान आंशिक रूप से बादलों से घिरा रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 40 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने की संभावना है।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, पूरे सप्ताह किसी भी दिन के लिए कोई विशेष चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। मौसम विशेषज्ञों का कहना है कि पश्चिमी विक्षोभ और स्थानीय मौसमी गतिविधियों के प्रभाव से बादलों की आवाजाही बढ़ी है। इसके चलते तापमान में अत्यधिक वृद्धि की संभावना फिलहाल कम है। तेज हवाओं और संभावित हल्की बारिश के कारण लोगों को उमस और भीषण गर्मी से राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है।
दोपहर बाद अचानक छाए घने बादलों और चल रही ठंडी हवाओं ने लोगों को राहत का एहसास कराया। मौसम विभाग का मानना है कि आने वाले दिनों में भी एनसीआर में मौसम अपेक्षाकृत नरम बना रहेगा और अधिकतम तापमान 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास ही रहने की संभावना है।

The weather office said the heatwave is affecting Mymensingh and Sylhet divisions, along with Dhaka, Tangail, Manikganj, Kishoreganj, Rajshahi, Sirajganj, Rangpur, Nilphamari, Chandpur, Feni, Jashore, Chuadanga, Kushtia, Satkhira, Khulna, Barishal and Patuakhali. The heat may ease in some areas.

Bandarban also recorded the highest rainfall in the country during the previous 24 hours, with 42 millimetres recorded up to 6am Wednesday.

BDO Singapore’s Roger Loo: Organisations that combine strategic agility with execution excellence will be most successful
He said that leaders must be capable of making informed decisions in increasingly complex environments.
In 2025, businesses in Singapore continued to place greater focus on strategic resilience, data-informed decision-making, and sustainable growth as they navigated evolving regional markets. Organisations continued to strengthen performance management and explore internationalisation opportunities to remain competitive.
These priorities closely align with the extensive background of BDO Singapore’s Dr Roger Loo, who has three decades of experience in business intelligence and management consulting. In his role, he has established a distinguished track record across diverse domains, including market intelligence, strategic advisory, feasibility studies, internationalisation, family enterprise development, and performance management.
As one of the judges in the Singapore Business Review Management Excellence Awards 2026, Loo explores the way organisations are redefining sustainable growth, identifying and addressing strategic blind spots, and adapting their decision-making approaches as artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more prominent. He also aims to understand developments that could shape Singapore’s business environment and the management capabilities organisations will need to sustain competitiveness in the near future.
Based on your work with companies in different markets, what shifts are you seeing in the way businesses define sustainable growth?
Sustainable growth is no longer defined purely by revenue and profitability. Increasingly, organisations are taking a more holistic view that balances financial performance with resilience, stakeholder trust, talent sustainability, digital capability, and responsible governance. We are seeing business leaders shift their focus from short-term gains towards building organisations that can adapt to market disruptions, regulatory changes, and evolving customer expectations.
Another notable shift is the growing emphasis on value creation rather than simple expansion. Companies are investing in digital transformation, operational efficiency, and customer experience improvements to drive long-term competitiveness. Sustainability itself has moved from a compliance exercise to a strategic agenda, with leading organisations integrating environmental, social, and governance considerations into core decision-making processes.
What strategic blind spots do you commonly observe amongst organisations today?
One of the most common blind spots is the tendency to focus heavily on operational performance whilst underestimating the speed of external change. Many organisations still rely on historical success factors despite significant shifts in customer behaviour, technology, workforce expectations, and competitive dynamics.
Another blind spot is the lack of integration between strategy and execution. We often see well-crafted strategic plans that are not adequately translated into measurable actions, governance structures, and performance indicators. In addition, many organisations underestimate talent and culture risks. Digital transformation, for example, is often treated as a technology initiative when it is fundamentally an organisational change programme that requires leadership alignment and workforce readiness.
How do you expect artificial intelligence to reshape strategic planning and business decision-making?
Artificial intelligence will fundamentally transform decision-making by enabling faster access to insights, predictive capabilities, and scenario-based planning. Traditionally, strategic planning has relied heavily on historical data and periodic reviews. AI allows organisations to continuously analyse market conditions, customer trends, operational performance, and emerging risks in near real time.
However, the most significant impact may not be automation itself but augmentation. AI will enhance the quality of executive decision-making by helping leaders evaluate multiple strategic options, identify patterns that may otherwise be missed, and improve forecasting accuracy. The organisations that achieve the greatest value will be those that combine AI-driven insights with strong human judgement, governance, and ethical oversight. Ultimately, AI should enable leaders to spend less time gathering information and more time focusing on innovation, growth, and stakeholder value creation.
What regional trends do you believe will have the greatest impact on Singapore businesses over the next few years?
Several regional trends are likely to shape Singapore's business landscape significantly. First, the continued restructuring of global and regional supply chains will create both opportunities and challenges as businesses seek greater resilience and diversification. Singapore is well-positioned to serve as a strategic hub for companies navigating these changes.
Second, the acceleration of digitalisation and AI adoption across Southeast Asia will intensify competition whilst creating new growth opportunities. Organisations will need to continuously innovate to maintain relevance and competitiveness.
Third, demographic shifts, talent shortages, and changing workforce expectations will increasingly influence business strategy. The ability to attract, develop, and retain skilled talent will become a critical differentiator. Finally, growing regulatory expectations around sustainability, governance, and data management will require organisations to strengthen compliance capabilities whilst leveraging these areas as sources of competitive advantage.
Looking ahead, what management capabilities do you believe organisations will need most to stay competitive over the next five years?
The most successful organisations will be led by management teams that combine strategic agility with execution excellence. Leaders must be capable of navigating uncertainty, responding quickly to market changes, and making informed decisions in increasingly complex environments.
Digital and AI literacy will also become essential management competencies. Leaders do not need to be technical experts, but they must understand how emerging technologies can generate value and transform business models. Equally important are capabilities related to change leadership, stakeholder management, and talent development. As organisations continue to evolve, leaders will need to foster cultures of innovation, adaptability, and continuous learning.
Ultimately, competitiveness will depend on an organisation's ability to align people, technology, and strategy around a common vision whilst maintaining strong governance and accountability.
As a returning judge for the Singapore Business Review Management Excellence Awards 2026, what new business trends are you hoping to see reflected in this year's award submissions?
I would be particularly interested in seeing examples of organisations that have moved beyond simply adopting new technologies to demonstrating measurable business outcomes from transformation initiatives. AI, digitalisation, and automation are important, but what truly matters is how these capabilities deliver tangible value for customers, employees, and shareholders.
I would also welcome submissions showcasing innovative approaches to workforce transformation, sustainability integration, and customer-centric business model innovation. The most compelling organisations are often those that successfully balance growth with resilience and long-term value creation.
Finally, I hope to see strong examples of leadership during periods of change. In today's environment, management excellence is not just about achieving impressive financial results; it is about building agile, purpose-driven organisations that can thrive amid uncertainty whilst creating lasting positive impact for all stakeholders.

A summer of high temperatures will lead to more potholes during winter, the RAC has warned.
Many parts of the UK experienced record temperatures during a summer frequented by heatwaves and it is these periods which will create even more potholes.
The RAC points towards the negative effect which UV rays have on the bitumen used to bind road materials together.
When exposed to long durations of high temperatures, this can cause asphalt to become brittle and break away when it cools.
RAC head of policy Simon Williams said: “As UV and heat oxidise the bitumen binder in asphalt, it becomes harder and less flexible which leads to cracking. Then water penetrates cracks and as vehicles drive over them, the surface breaks and potholes start to appear. This is the last thing our already fragile roads needed.”
A recent Report on Motoring conducted by the RAC spoke to 2,238 drivers and found that half of drivers saw potholes as their biggest worry, up from 47 per cent last year.
Some 83 per cent of drivers say they encounter a pothole on most trips they make by car, while more than half come across potholes on every trip. In addition, 58 per cent say that they have to make an effort to avoid them on every trip.
Williams added: “Potholes are often associated with cold or wet winters, but prolonged periods of hot, sunny weather also takes its toll on the roads. Intense UV exposure and heat gradually oxidise the bitumen that binds asphalt together, making surfaces more brittle and prone to cracking.
“Once cracks develop, traffic and later rainfall can quickly turn them into serious defects.:

On Saturday, Sept. 12, the SMU Mustangs defeated the UC Davis Aggies at their first home football game, as temperatures reached nearly 100 degrees Fahrenheit in Gerald J. Ford Stadium by kickoff at 3 p.m.
Despite the severe heat, 29,054 fans showed up to support the Mustangs, although many struggled to stay for the entirety of the game because of the conditions. Kickoff temperatures reached 99 degrees Fahrenheit.
“During Saturday’s SMU football game, the University Park Fire Department had 54 patient contacts and transported nine patients to local hospitals. The majority of these incidents and transports were related to heat-related illnesses,” said Paige Ruedy, the community information officer for University Park police, in an email to The Daily Campus.
Elisa Zairick, a third-year student, left the stadium roughly 20 minutes after the game started.
“It’s impossible to stay the whole game,” Zairick said. “We should have an enclosed stadium with AC; people wouldn’t leave early and would be more comfortable.”
For some fans, the heat became an issue before they entered the stadium. Sophomore Nicole Sauerbrey said one of her friends became dizzy before the game started, and had to be taken back to her dorm room.
“I don’t think SMU takes the correct measures to prevent students from dehydrating,” Sauerbrey said. “I think the stadium should be closed with air conditioning. I don’t think it’s healthy for the cheerleaders or players.”
As people exited the stadium, Cristina, a security supervisor, described how attendees were handling the weather conditions.
“For those who are not from Texas, this is like a tremendous heat wave,” she said.
The Texas heat can be hard to adjust to, especially considering many students are from out-of-state. SMU’s Fall 2025 enrollment shows that California, Florida, New York and Illinois are among the states with the highest number of students after Texas. These states don’t often experience intense heat waves.
Many students carried fans and water to avoid dehydration. Sport management student Anneliese Garcia brought an electric fan to prepare.
“I put on sunblock before coming, have sunglasses in my purse and brought an electric fan, but I don’t think it’s gonna be enough,” Garcia said.
Brooke Barnes, a former member of the SMU pom team, experienced the game from the stands for the first time; however, she recalls the heat from her days on the field.
“It was pretty tough to manage when you’re exercising in the heat for four hours straight,” Barnes said. “I would prepare by drinking lots of water the day before and taking Liquid I.V. to get those electrolytes in. I don’t think SMU prepares us, but we got to prepare ourselves.”
The heat also affected members of the Mustang Band. Drum major Garhett Daves said SMU Athletics encouraged the band to leave the stadium halfway through the third quarter, as members began experiencing symptoms of heat exhaustion.
In an unusual move for the band, Daves and other student leadership decided to return to the band hall to cool down before coming back for the end of the game. Members also changed out of their traditional uniforms and into polos and shorts before returning to the stadium.
“Being the best dressed band in the land, we don’t really have much of an outfit for these environments,” Daves said. “We always want to look our best and look sharp. But sometimes it’s a little too much.”
Daves, a junior who has been in the band since his freshman year, said Saturday was the hottest game he has experienced during his time with the Mustang Band.
Dallas will continue to experience temperatures in the 90s for the rest of September. SMU’s next home game is scheduled for Sept. 26 with a later kickoff at 8 p.m. Students can take precautions by staying hydrated, wearing sunscreen and taking breaks from the heat whenever needed.

Extreme fire danger after Darwin's hottest day of the year
A fire weather warning for extreme fire danger in the Darwin and Adelaide River district of the Northern Territory is in effect this Wednesday, as numerous fires burn in the immediate vicinity of the NT capital.
The NT government has two main categories for non-structural fires in the outdoors – bushfires, and grass and scrub fires – and both types of fires were burning this Wednesday.
Image: Bushfire smoke can be seen near Katherine and southeast of Darwin at 2 pm (ACST) on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, Source: Weatherzone.
Let's take a look at the short-term and long-term weather conditions in Darwin which have fuelled today's extreme fire danger near the city.
Seasonal factors: dry season was even drier than usual
While minimal rainfall is expected during the middle of the year in Darwin, the city has still received less than usual to date in the 2026 dry season.
- As of this Wednesday, September 16, Darwin has received just 7 mm of rainfall since the commencement of the official dry season on May 1.
- May typically sees 20.0 mm of rainfall on average, but Darwin received just 2.2 mm.
- Rainfall in what southerners call the "winter" months of June, July and August is almost negligible in Darwin. But it's still worth mentioning that both July and August were bone dry in Darwin this year.
- So far in September, just 1.8 mm of rainfall has been recorded. The long-term monthly average is 16.8 mm.
- Darwin’s average monthly maximums and minimums were both around one degree above average during each of June, July and August.
The above differences from the average are relatively marginal (especially the rainfall deficiencies, given you are starting from such a low base).
But these factors have nonetheless dried out the Top End landscape a little more than usual.
This week's weather: southeasterly winds bring heat to the Top End
Darwin hit 36°C on Sunday, its hottest day of the year to date, while this Wednesday marks the seventh straight day that Darwin's maximum has exceeded September's average high of 32.7°C by at least a degree.
Interestingly, the same weather system which has pushed chilly winds to the southeast corner of the country is largely responsible for Wednesday's extreme Top End fire danger.
Image: Synoptic chart for September 16, 2026. Source: Weatherzone.
In the wake of a cold front that passed over the southeast corner of the country, air circulating anti-clockwise around the high pressure system continues to funnel chilly air with polar origins onto Tasmania and the southeastern mainland.
But as the air moves inland and continues to circulate around the high, it gains warmth from the interior of the continent and is very warm by the time it reaches the Top End.
Southeasterly winds are also gusty in the Top End this Wednesday, with gusts exceeding 50 km/h recorded in most NT forecast districts.
It all adds up to the classic recipe for Top End fire danger, and with more hot weather and no significant rain on the horizon for the next week, it's likely that further fire danger warnings will be issued.
You can monitor the location and status of fires on the NT Fire Incident Map.
